pages.x: When Adolf Hitler took power in 1933, Germany's half a million Jews were thrown out of government jobs and their shops were boycotted. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 took away their citizenship and banned marriage with other Germans. Many fled, but other countries let in few refugees.

On the night of 9 November 1938 Nazi mobs across Germany and Austria burned hundreds of synagogues, smashed thousands of Jewish shops and homes and killed scores of Jews, and some 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. Afterwards Britain took in 10,000 Jewish children on the Kindertransport.

After conquering Poland, the Nazis forced its Jews into walled ghettos. In Warsaw some 400,000 people were packed into a few square kilometres, and tens of thousands died of hunger and typhus. In April 1943, as the last of them were being sent to their deaths, young Jewish fighters rose up and held out for a month.

From 1941 SS killing squads shot Jews by the hundred thousand in the conquered Soviet lands. In January 1942 Nazi officials met at Wannsee to plan what they called the final solution. Jews from all over Europe were sent by train to death camps in Poland, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec and Auschwitz, and murdered in gas chambers.
pages.of: Jews murdered, two in three in Europe

pages.x: Anne Frank, a Jewish girl in Amsterdam, hid with her family for two years in rooms behind her father's office, and kept a diary of her hopes and fears. In August 1944 they were betrayed and sent to the camps. Anne died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen early in 1945, aged 15. Her father, the only one to survive, published her diary.

pages.t: Others they killed, and those who helped
pages.x: The Nazis also murdered Roma and Sinti people, perhaps a quarter of a million or more, disabled people, millions of Soviet prisoners and Polish civilians, and political enemies and gay men. Some people risked everything to help: in 1943 Danish fishermen ferried almost all of Denmark's Jews to safety in Sweden.

As the Allies advanced, the SS drove prisoners on death marches. Soviet soldiers reached Auschwitz on 27 January 1945 and found some 7,000 prisoners left behind. British and American troops reaching Bergen-Belsen, Buchenwald and Dachau found piles of bodies and starving survivors, and their photographs showed the world.

The Holocaust was the largest genocide in history, planned and carried out by a modern state. Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg, and the world made genocide a crime. 27 January, the day Auschwitz was freed, is now Holocaust Remembrance Day, and survivors' words still ask the world never to forget.
